---
title: "How to contribute to animovement"
toc: true
---

The ecosystem of *animovement* packages would not be possible without the
contributions of the R community. No matter your current skills, it's possible
to contribute back to *animovement*. Contributions are guided by our design
goals.

## Design goals

The goals of *animovement* packages are to:

- Encourage empirical validation and good statistical practice.
- Smooth out heterogeneous interfaces.
- Establish highly reusable infrastructure.
- Enable a wider variety of methodologies.
- Help package developers quickly build high quality movement packages of their
  own.

These goals are guided by our principles for creating movement analysis
packages.

## Answer questions

You can help others use and learn *animovement* by answering questions on our
[Zulip chat](https://animovement.zulipchat.com). Many people asking for help
don't know what a reprex is or how to craft one. Acknowledging someone's
problem, showing them how to build a *reprex*, and pointing them to helpful
resources are all enormously beneficial, even if you don't immediately solve
their problem.

Remember that while you might have seen a problem a hundred times before, it's
new to the person asking it. Be patient, polite, and empathic.

## File issues {#sec-issues}

Bug reports and feature requests are both welcome. Each package tracks its
issues in its own repository on [GitHub](https://github.com/animovement), so
file yours on the package concerned. If you're not sure which one that is, use
the [animovement](https://github.com/animovement/animovement/issues)
repository and we'll move it.

For a bug, first create a minimal reprex. Spend some time working to make it as
minimal as possible; the more time you spend doing this, the easier it is to
fix the bug. For a feature request, describe the problem it would solve, not
only the solution you have in mind. Each repository's issue form asks for
what's needed.

The *animovement* team is small (currently I'm a one-man team - hi!). I often
focus on one package at a time to reduce context switching and be more
efficient. We may not address each issue right away, but we will use the reprex
you create to understand your problem when it is time to focus on that package.

## Contribute documentation

Documentation is a high priority for *animovement*, and pull requests to correct
or improve it are welcome. It comes in two kinds:

- **Function documentation** lives in the R source files, as
  [roxygen2](https://roxygen2.r-lib.org) comments next to the code it
  describes, written in markdown.
- **Articles** teach how to use the packages. The ones that span several
  packages, such as the [Get Started](../get-started/index.qmd) guides and the
  [Learn](../learn/index.qmd) tutorials, live on this site; the ones about a
  single package live on that package's own site.

We'd be particularly happy to receive real-life examples, for instance from
research articles, that use *animovement*. Add them as new Quarto files
(`.qmd`) in the *Learn* folder of the
[website's repository](https://github.com/animovement/animovement.github.io).

## Contribute code

If you'd like to contribute to package development directly, start by filing
an issue, and wait until we've agreed on the idea and the basic approach before
opening a pull request. That saves both of us work.

The [contributing guide](https://github.com/animovement/.github/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md)
has everything else. It is shared by every package. In short:

- Code follows the [tidyverse style guide](https://style.tidyverse.org) and is
  formatted with [air](https://posit-dev.github.io/air/).
- Every change comes with tests, and a `NEWS.md` bullet when users will notice
  it.
- Pull request titles follow
  [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org), such as
  `fix(animetric): keep metadata through summarise_path()`.

If you use AI tools, please read our
[AI policy](https://github.com/animovement/.github/blob/main/AI.md) first. You
can use them, but you have to understand and have tested everything you
submit.

### Working with an AI assistant

The **`animovement-dev`** agent skill teaches an AI assistant such as
[Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) how the packages are developed:
the conventions above, how releases and versions work, and the decisions that
aren't written down anywhere else. In Claude Code:

```
/plugin marketplace add animovement/animovement-agents
/plugin install animovement@animovement
```

Other assistants can use the same skills; see
[animovement-agents](https://github.com/animovement/animovement-agents) for how.

The *animovement* packages are built to support other movement analysis tools,
and we would love to hear about what you build yourself!
